content: The studies reviewed in this recommendation are detailed in Appendix 4. For the outcome of births attended by skilled birth attendants or facility-based births, the quality of evidence was rated as very low. Only one study from Bangladesh (Hossain and Ross, 2006) reported on this outcome. The study design was not clearly stated but appeared to be a quasi-experimental pre-and-post study with a control group. The intervention included multiple components, such as community mobilization and quality-of-care improvements. The results indicated significant increases in facility births in the intervention and comparison areas, but not in the control area. However, the evidence quality was very low. For the outcome of care provided by skilled birth attendants or in facilities during maternal complications, the evidence quality was also rated as very low. The same study (Hossain and Ross, 2006) reported significant increases in the number of women with obstetric complications receiving care in emergency obstetric care (EmOC) facilities in the intervention and comparison areas, but not in the control area. Errors in the reported outcome data and unclear survey sample sizes further weakened the evidence. Implementation considerations were informed by a background document by Howard-Grabman (2014), which reviewed the context and conditions of the programs described in the studies. Lessons learned from maternal death surveillance and response (MDSR) processes highlight the importance of community participation, which adds complexity. Key lessons include the value of maternal death reviews in raising awareness of challenges and stimulating discussions for solutions. Community members may participate as family informants in maternal and perinatal death inquiries and in presenting summary data to identify ways to improve health outcomes. Tools such as the three-delays framework and verbal autopsy are useful in maternal death reviews. Notification of maternal deaths can be challenging but may improve over time as communities become aware of the importance of collecting this information. Both health providers and communities require preparation to work together, and this process involves learning and trust-building. Community involvement may initially heighten fears of recrimination among providers, and communities may be reluctant to discuss sensitive topics like death and pregnancy due to strong cultural beliefs. In countries with advanced maternal and perinatal death reviews, near-miss reviews should be added to explore how communities can help prevent future problems. This should be done sensitively, considering the circumstances of the death and cultural practices around pregnancy and childbirth. Processes often evolve and improve over time as experience and confidence grow. It may be best to start with simpler maternal death reviews, then add perinatal death reviews, and eventually progress to near-miss reviews. All partners should be aware that better reporting may initially result in higher apparent mortality rates as notification systems improve. Mapping deaths by physical location can help target program attention and interventions. Despite insufficient evidence to make a strong recommendation, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) found this intervention promising, particularly in improving accountability. Further research is needed to determine the best ways to implement the intervention in different contexts and to study its processes and effects. Areas for investigation include understanding the interaction between interviewers and respondents when gathering information on deaths, identifying who should collect the information, and determining how communities can best participate in discussions. Lessons from community involvement in neonatal death reviews could also be applied. Planned interventions must address the possibility that healthcare providers may fear recrimination if communities are involved in reviews. Nearly all quality-improvement frameworks include community/user perspectives as key elements. In maternity services, women’s and community perspectives are essential in defining good-quality care. This intervention aligns with the broader interest in increased accountability. Ensuring community participation in analyzing information and identifying solutions can help services respond better to community needs. Community members may participate in quality reviews as informants or in discussions about healthcare information to identify ways to improve services. Mechanisms such as consultations with communities, community representation on health facility management committees, and meetings between community representatives, service managers, and providers are recommended. The prevention and elimination of disrespect and abuse during facility-based childbirth are critical. Community participation in quality improvement can take various forms, such as stakeholder quality-improvement committees or facilitated dialogue sessions involving representatives from both the community and health services. Collaboration between community members and service providers to jointly define and improve quality can be effective when supported by a well-facilitated dialogue process that considers diverse perspectives. Pregnant women’s voices must be included, and there should be adequate diversity in the perspectives of community members and service providers. Quality-improvement committees can support ongoing collaboration when all members understand and commit to the group’s purpose, roles, and responsibilities are clear and acceptable, and governance practices support participation. Joint assessments of health services and care can inform decision-making, and ongoing monitoring of data can guide strategy adaptation for continual improvement and accountability. Health facility leadership that supports collaboration with communities is essential for this approach to be effective. This intervention should be seen as a dynamic process. Building trust between different actors and developing their capacity to plan and work together takes time. Data must be presented in ways that are understandable to all participants, effectively communicating health issues to those within and outside the health sector with varying levels of education and experience. While NGOs may have experience facilitating community involvement, their work should be linked to government services and embedded in ongoing processes where they exist. It is important to include voices and perspectives from diverse community groups. The GDG identified several research gaps, including understanding the dynamics of community-service interfaces in various settings, community/provider action planning processes, accessible ways of presenting data to highlight progress and trends, community feedback on services, and mechanisms for providers to give feedback to communities. Advocacy’s role in improving service quality and the effects of participation on community dynamics, self-efficacy, identity, and power relations also require further study. Lessons from high-income countries and their applicability to other settings should also be assessed.
